## Overview

The Hunkpapa (Lakota: *Húŋkpapȟa*) are one of the seven council fires of the Lakota tribe. Their name means “Head of the Circle,” referring to their traditional position at the entryway to the circle of the Great Council when the Sioux met in convocation. They speak Lakȟóta, one of the three dialects of the Sioux language. Historically, Hunkpapa territory extended from the Big Cheyenne to the Yellowstone and west to the Black Hills; since the 1880s, most Hunkpapa have lived in the Standing Rock Sioux Reservation in North and South Dakota, along the Grand River. The Hunkpapa were involved in conflicts and treaties with the United States during the nineteenth century, including the Battle of Little Bighorn in July 1876. By 1891, about 571 Hunkpapa Lakota resided in the reservation.

## Material culture

### Architecture

The sources identify lodges and tipis as Hunkpapa camp dwellings. Hunkpapa camps were traditionally arranged within the circle of the Great Council, with the Húŋkpapȟa at the entryway.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They mention a medal given to Little White Bear by United States representatives in connection with the treaty of 1825.

## Music & performance

They identify Robert “Tree” Cody as a flutist and Ernie LaPointe as a Sun dancer, author, and orator.

## Dance & theatre

They identify Ernie LaPointe as a Sun dancer, without describing the dance itself, its ceremonial context, or its performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources mention Sitting Bull College president Tomi Kay Phillips, whose name is given as Cante Wakan Win, and identify Ernie LaPointe as a Sun dancer, but provide no ritual account.

## Foodways

The sources mention buffalo as an important reason for Lakota movement and occupation of hunting grounds.

## Oral tradition & literature

They identify Hunkpapa artists, writers, authors, poets, orators, and ledger artists, including Barbara May Cameron, Ćehu′pa, Dana Claxton, Annie Little Warrior, and Ernie LaPointe. The sources also identify Hunkpapa winter count keeper Ćehu′pa and describe him as a Ledger Art artist.

## Language & religion

The Hunkpapa speak Lakȟóta, one of the three dialects of the Sioux language. The name *Húŋkpapȟa* is identified as a Lakota word meaning “Head of the Circle.”

commons_photos.title: Circling Bear, Hunkpapa Sioux, in a Feathered Headdress Holding a Pipe and Club (543418726c274bb985378f329deeddfe).tif
commons_photos.credit: Unknown Photographer (Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument)
commons_photos.description:
LIBI_00312_11185; Mounted albumen card. This portrait depicts Circling Bear, a Hunkpapa Sioux, in full length left profile. He is wearing a long, feathered headdress. He has a club in his right hand and a pipe in his left. The pipe bag is also visible. “Barry” is printed on the image and “Circling Bear.” is handwritten in the bottom left corner. A white label typed in blue ink reads: “No. 5. Hunkpapa Sioux Circling Bear (Mato Aohomniya), in War Dress.”  A handwritten note in ink on the verso reads: “Circling Bear”. This image was created by an unknown photographer, probably Barry, circa 1880. ; album photograph;Courtesy of the National Park Service, Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument, LIBI_00312_11185, Unknown Photographer, "Circling Bear, Hunkpapa Sioux, in a Feathered Headdress Holding a Pipe and Club," circa 1880.
Keywords: native american

commons_photos.credit: D. F. Barry (Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument)
commons_photos.description:
LIBI_00312_11187; Albumen cabinet photograph. This portrait depicts Crow King, a Hunkpapa Sioux. He is seated in front view. He is wearing a U.S. Army Jacket and a bone breast plate. His braids are covered in fur. There is one feather in his hair, cocked to the right. The background is very fuzzy. A white rectangle appears between the subject’s hands. The words “Crow King”, barely visible, are printed on it. “Barry” is printed on the image and on the mount. A handwritten note in orange on the verso reads: “Crow King.” This image was created by D.F. Barry in 1881. It is an original image. ; album, photograph;Courtesy of the National Park Service, Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument, LIBI_00312_11187, D. F. Barry, "Crow King in an Army Jacket and Bone Breast Plate," 1881.
Keywords: native american; sitting bull
